newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar, jet fuel price hit SIA.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar, jet fuel price hit SIA.

text.p: A strong Singapore dollar and the price of jet fuel are affecting Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA)'s performance, deputy chairman and chief executive officer Cheong Choong Kong said on Wednesday.

In an interview with Reuters, Cheong said performance in the first half was affected by the weak yen, rising jet fuel prices and a weak cargo market, factors which have continued into the second half.

Earlier this week the group reported an 11.4 percent drop in operating pre-tax profit to Singapore $468 million (US$332 million) in the first half ended September 30, 1996. Sales of aircraft and spares lifted group net profit by 7.2 percent to S$561 million.
Cheong declined to give any forecast for the group's second half performance.
On the cargo front, traffic growth has not kept pace with capacity. Cargo capacity went up by close to 15 percent but loads only went up about 12 percent.

Cheong said he does not see the weak cargo market bottoming in the next two months and that would depend on whether there was a pick up in exports, especially of electronic items, in Asia Pacific economies in the first quarter of next year.
SIA cargo capacity should stabilise next year as there are no plans to add any new freighters, Cheong added.
On the passenger front, traffic rose but yields fell due to the strong Singapore dollar and keen competition.
Local yields in overseas markets were depressed mainly due to the strength of the Singapore dollar against foreign currencies like the yen and mark.
"We lost in the first half SS$90 million due to the strong Singapore dollar," Cheong said.
"The weakness of the yen cost us a lot because the Japanese market is a big market for us."
Cheong said it was difficult to predict where the yen was heading. "The Japanese yen seems to be dropping without any bottom and that is frightening."
He said jet fuel prices also look uncertain and would depend on the winter's severity in Europe and North America.
SIA traditionally hedges some of its fuel requirements and that saved the airline some S$20 million in the first half.

Cheong said SIA has not been able to hedge jet fuel oil requirements much in the second half because prices have risen too sharply. "We have not been able to hedge -- it was too costly. Fuel prices were rising too fast."
Singapore jet fuel prices are currently around US$30.50 per barrel, having risen by over 30 percent year-on-year.
Cheong said SIA expects passenger growth (in capacity terms) of about eight percent annually and cargo by a slightly higher rate over the next five years.
A proposed joint-venture with the Tata Industries group in India to operate a domestic airline there was still on hold as the was still no official reply from the Indian government.
Cheong said SIA was looking to form joint ventures in other countries but declined to give details.
Regarding current subsidiaries, he said SilkAir might break even this year after a small first-half loss of S$3 million.
There were no plans to float the highly profitable SIA Engineering and Singapore Airport Terminal Services Group (SATS) as SIA has no need for the cash.
